newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity takes its message directly to investors.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity takes its message directly to investors.

text.p: Fidelity Investments' top executives, armed with a new strategic alliance with Salomon Brothers and sweeping changes among its fund managers, went on the offensive Tuesday in the first of six meetings with the company's leading clients.

Stung by negative publicity in the past year and a dwindling share of new assets under management, Fidelity took its case directly to its most senior clients, holding closed-door meetings in New York's Waldorf-Astoria Hotel.

"They've recognized that a lot of the stuff that has happened in the past year, and they've taken a more defensive tact to the issue," said Eric Kobren, editor of Fidelity Insight, a newsletter that follows the company. "I applaud them for getting out their message and talking directly to shareholders."

That message entails a variety of new services and funds, most of which are designed to compete directly with rivals that have become increasingly threatening to the once-dominant Fidelity. The Boston-based mutual fund company will also trumpet its efforts to shore up the managment of its stock funds, many of which put in poor performances last year.

Among its recent moves, Fidelity last week announced a deal with Salomon Brothers, a unit of Salomon Inc, to offer its discount brokerage customers up to 10 percent of any initial public or secondary offerings lead-managed by Salomon.
Also as part of that arrangement, Fidelity customers will gain access to Salomon's research, a step up from Fidelity's limited RealTime Research Package.

The Salomon alliance and Fidelity's plans to expand its Funds Network mutual fund supermarket are seen as an effort to counter Charles Schwab & Co Inc's discount brokerage service and Schwab's popular OneSource online trading and research site on the Internet's World Wide Web, analysts said.
Meanwhile, Fidelity plans to start new index funds this year, adding to a bond index fund and three equity funds that track the Standard & Poor's 500.

That move is intended to counter the Vanguard Group, whose index funds took market share from Fidelity last year. For the first time in 1996, Vanguard mutual funds took in more new cash than Fidelity funds, according to analysts.
And the $32.5 billion Vanguard Index 500 Portfolio, which tracks the S&P 500, outperformed all but about five of Fidelity's U.S. diversified stock funds in 1996.

"A billion dollars a week has been coming into index funds, and that's Vanguard and others, and they (Fidelity) want to make sure they get a piece of that," said Don Dion, publisher of Fidelity Independent Advisor.
Fidelity plans to cut fees on its bond mutual funds, too.
During the past year, the company made extensive changes in the management of its stock funds after the departure of many portfolio managers.

Fidelity executives scheduled to participate in the meetings include Gary Burkhead, head of Fidelity Management and Research and the number two in command. Paul Hondros, who heads up Fidelity's retail products, and Robert Reynolds, who oversees retirement programs, will also take part. Several fund managers will also give presentations, Fidelity said.

Dion said he expected the executives to tell their customers the fund company had a solid portfolio management team despite the defections, and that the funds would stick to their investment objectives after a disastrous 1996 for some of their funds. They may also outline steps to keep more managers from leaving, he said.
"They are clearly on the offensive; they have sort of come out of their shell," Dion said, noting that many of the executives are making themselves more available to the media.
After the all-day meeting in New York, Fidelity will open a session for retail customers to the media at 1830 EST/2330 GMT.
After the New York meeting, the Fidelity executives will travel to Atlanta on Wednesday, then Dallas, San Francisco and Chicago. The tour is scheduled to end in Boston on January 30.
